greek.title: Epicurus and the Garden of Pleasures
greek.body:
In 307 BCE, Epicurus purchased a small garden outside Athens and established a philosophical school that would scandalize the city. While other philosophers met in gymnasia or colonnaded walkways, Epicurus welcomed students to his κῆπος—including women and slaves, a radical breach of convention.

His doctrine of ἡδονή shocked contemporaries who expected hedonism to mean wild excess. Instead, Epicurus taught that true pleasure was freedom from pain and mental disturbance. The greatest pleasures? Bread, water, friendship, and philosophical conversation. His community shared simple meals and avoided political life entirely.

Critics branded them atheists and libertines. Yet Epicurus kept a strict regimen, eating barley cakes and occasionally splurging on cheese. When he died, he left his garden to his followers in perpetuity, ensuring that generations could pursue what he called "the pleasure of a settled stomach and a tranquil mind."
